name: Gaura Parva
when: Aug–Sep, from Bhadra Krishna Panchami, about 4–5 days
summary: Gaura is the biggest festival of Nepal's far west, celebrating the goddess Gaura (Parvati) and her marriage to Maheshwar (Shiva). Married women soak five grains, fast and worship, and villages sing Deuda songs and dance in circles for several days in late summer.
body: Gaura is celebrated across Sudurpashchim Province, in parts of Karnali Province and across the border in Kumaon in Uttarakhand. It begins on Biruda Panchami, the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Bhadra, when married women soak five kinds of grains, the biruda, in a copper or brass vessel. Over the following days the grains are washed at a spring or stream, offered to the deities and later shared as prasad, and women fast and pray for the well-being of their husbands and families.

Figures of Gaura and Maheshwar are made from grasses, plants and cloth, dressed and decorated, and carried to a community courtyard called the Gaura khalo or Gaura ghar. There they are worshipped over several days as the divine couple, with songs that tell the story of Gaura's marriage. Women wear their finest saris and jewellery, often with red dresses and gold nose rings typical of the far west, and young girls take part alongside married women.

The evenings belong to music. Men and women form circles to sing Deuda, the call-and-response folk songs of the region, and to dance the Deuda and other local dances, sometimes late into the night. Songs range from devotional to witty exchanges about love, migration and village life. In Dhangadhi and the hill towns, the festival has also become a stage for cultural programmes and a public holiday in the province.
tips: Ask a local guide to take you to a village Gaura khalo rather than only a staged town event.
Dress modestly and ask before photographing women during rituals.
Expect monsoon rain and road delays in the hills; base yourself in Dhangadhi or Dipayal.

faqs.a: Gaura begins on Bhadra Krishna Panchami in the Nepali lunar calendar, which falls in late August or early September, and lasts about four to five days, ending around Gaura Ashtami. Exact dates change every year with the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel and confirm with local sources.

Married women soak five grains (biruda), fast and worship Gaura and Maheshwar. Figures of the divine couple are made from plants and cloth, dressed and carried to a community courtyard, where they are worshipped for several days. Evenings bring Deuda singing and circle dancing by men and women.

faqs.q: Where is the best place to see Gaura Parva?
faqs.a: Anywhere in Sudurpashchim Province, including Dhangadhi, Dadeldhura, Doti, Baitadi and the hill districts. Villages show the most traditional form, with rituals at the local Gaura khalo, while Dhangadhi holds larger public programmes. A local guide makes it far easier to join respectfully.

Yes, visitors are generally welcome to watch and often invited to join the Deuda circles in the evening. Be respectful during rituals, which are religious and mainly for married women, and ask before taking photographs. A small offering or contribution to the community event is appreciated.

name: Maghi, the Tharu New Year
when: Mid-January, from Magh 1 (Maghe Sankranti), several days
summary: Maghi is the most important festival of the Tharu people of the western Terai, marking their new year on the first of the Nepali month of Magh, around 14–15 January. Villages around Bardia, Dhangadhi and Shuklaphanta celebrate with feasts, dances, family visits and the choosing of village leaders.
body: For most Nepalis, the first day of Magh is Maghe Sankranti, the day the sun turns north and people eat sesame sweets, yam and ghee. For the Tharu of Bardia, Kailali, Kanchanpur, Banke and Dang, the same day begins Maghi, their new year and the largest festival of the year. Celebrations last several days, and Tharu people working elsewhere in Nepal and India travel home to join their families.

The festival begins with bathing in rivers at dawn and offerings to ancestors, followed by feasts that feature pork, fish, freshwater snails, dhikri rice dumplings and home-brewed rice drinks. Young people visit elders to receive blessings, and families settle debts and plans for the coming year. Traditionally, Maghi is also when villages choose their Badghar, the village headman, and agree on shared work such as irrigation and festivals.

Evenings bring dancing. Groups of young men and women in Tharu dress, with white or coloured skirts, beads and silver jewellery, perform circle dances to drums and songs, moving from house to house. In Thakurdwara near Bardia National Park and in Dhangadhi, public programmes add stage performances and fairs. January is cool and foggy in the Terai, but safari season is under way, so Maghi fits neatly into a Bardia trip.
tips: Plan a Bardia safari around 14–17 January to see Maghi in Tharu villages near the park.
Bring warm layers; January mornings in the Terai are foggy and around 7–10 °C.
Accept food and drink politely, but it is fine to decline alcohol with a smile.

faqs.q: When is the Tharu Maghi festival?
faqs.a: Maghi starts on Magh 1 in the Nepali calendar, usually 14 or 15 January, the same day as Maghe Sankranti. Celebrations in Tharu villages last several days, sometimes up to a week. The government declares a public holiday in the Tharu-majority districts. Check current status before you travel for the exact date.

faqs.q: Where can I see Maghi celebrations?
faqs.a: In Tharu villages across Bardia, Banke, Kailali, Kanchanpur and Dang. Around Thakurdwara at Bardia National Park, lodges can arrange village visits during the festival. Dhangadhi holds larger public events with stage dances. Village celebrations are more personal and authentic, with house-to-house dancing.

faqs.q: What food is eaten at Maghi?
faqs.a: Pork, fish, freshwater snails and crab, dhikri rice-flour dumplings, sweet potatoes and yam, sesame sweets and home-brewed rice drinks. Families prepare food for days, and guests are offered generous helpings. Vegetarians can enjoy dhikri, yam, sesame laddoos and vegetable dishes.

faqs.q: Why is Maghi important to the Tharu?
faqs.a: Maghi is the Tharu new year, a time for family reunion, honouring ancestors, receiving blessings from elders and planning the year ahead. Traditionally, villages also choose their Badghar, the village headman, at Maghi. It is the main expression of Tharu identity and culture in the western Terai.
